title: They Don’t Make ’Em Like They Used to, and Maybe That’s OK

body_markdown:
Back in the 1960s, the vigilant, if not easily amused, engineers at *Consumer Reports* published lists of delivery defects on all new cars purchased for testing. A helpful if somewhat scary practice, the lists were often longer than you might expect, and they included everything from missing trim bits, to a Ford Cortina that turned more sharply in one direction than the other. (The problem turned out to be a steering box that left the factory missing an installation bolt or two.)


*CR’s* April 1966 Auto issue includes a lengthy list of such defects, some more concerning than others. All receive equal billing, whether a defective brake-light switch or a malfunctioning windshield-washer pump. And all are delivered in *CR’s* unemotional, matter-of-fact style:


- Transmission fluid leak
- Power steering hose badly chafed by fan belt—almost worn through
- Rain leaks (several cars)
- Shock absorber mounting broken off
- Mechanical rapping noises in engine
- Engine block defective, requiring replacement
- Carburetor overflowing gasoline
- One end of front stabilizer bar disconnected; link missing


Curiously, no mention is made of any follow-up or fixes, leaving one to wonder what happened next. By the looks of it, some of the issues might have best been solved with a quick visit to the crusher.


Reading these lists 60 years later, the tired expression that insists that “They don’t make them like they used to” inevitably comes to mind. It’s a particularly popular sentiment in old car circles, and the saying is true on many levels. Cars weren’t necessarily better, safer, or more reliable “back then.” In fact, it’s pretty easy to make the case that the opposite is true.


In the days before SUVs ruled suburban roads, station wagons were the family utility vehicles of choice.


Consumer Reports


An engineer checking the controls and driver’s seating position in the 1950s.


Consumer Reports


Consumer expectations were lower back in the day, and Detroit was more than ready to lower the bar; in the ’60s, build quality was sometimes notoriously shoddy. Breakdowns were far more common than they are today, and a car was more of a disposable commodity. Many buyers traded in every year, or as soon as their old ride was paid off two or three years later. Nobody envisioned a day when the average age of all cars on the road sits at over 12 years, as it is today. The notion of buying anything with more than 50,000 miles on the clock was often described as buying someone else’s problems.


“Cars are definitely more reliable than they were in the ’60s,” said Jake Fisher, senior director of auto testing for *Consumer Reports* . ”In those days, an odometer turned over to zero at 100,000 miles, because they weren’t expected to go over 100,000 miles. Now, if you’re buying a used car with 100,000 miles, depending on what it is, you’re likely to say, ‘Oh, there’s plenty of life in it.’”


For years, one measure of a station wagon’s worth was how easily it could accommodate a 4×8 sheet of plywood. Here, a 1957 Ford Country Sedan is put to the test.


Consumer Reports


Granted, the 1960s were a simpler time, with simpler cars. While that’s not an excuse to improperly bolt on a steering box or to send a defective engine block out into the world, it does mean that at least most of *CR’s* defects were easily remedied by a visit to the dealer. Some could have easily been fixed by a home mechanic.


Anyone who has ever had to pay to replace a modern infotainment screen will tell you that the same is not always the case with today’s cars, with their sophisticated electronics. The flip side is that electronic advancements have played a huge role in making new cars both safer and more reliable. But that doesn’t mean they’re without issues.


Fun-loving engineers take a break from testing early SUVs from the 1960s. Left to right: Checker Marathon, International Travelall, and Chevrolet Suburban.


Consumer Reports


“We purchase about 50 cars every year for testing,” said Fisher, “and we absolutely see defects. Very often these cars are going back to the dealer and getting fixed, sometimes multiple times.


“Sometimes, we have trouble just making sure the car is running correctly when we’re doing our tests. We used to see problems with the steering, or problems with an engine. You could fix those, and you could replicate those. Electronic problems can be very intermittent and hard to fix. A computer glitching? You may not be able to replicate that.”


Changing a tire is made easier thanks to the hydropneumatic suspension on this Citroën DS.


Consumer Reports


A modern car has anywhere from 1400 to as many as 3000 separate microprocessors, according to Bloomington, Minnesota’s Polar Semiconductor, which has been supplying semiconductors to the automotive industry for the last 50 years. By comparison, that figure was zero in the 1960s. While there is no question that advances brought by Mr. Microchip, like electronic ignition and fuel injection, have helped make today’s cars more reliable than anything from the 1960s, those advances have also led to systems far beyond the capabilities of the typical shadetree mechanic.


“The types of problems that you are going to have today weren’t around in the ’60s,” adds Fisher, like issues with an infotainment system or a fussy Bluetooth pairing system.


Family cars like this 1963 Plymouth Valiant have long been a staple of *CR* testing.


Consumer Reports


That’s not to say that infotainment systems aren’t a good thing, or that similar electronic advancements in braking, steering, and safety systems aren’t real lifesavers. It’s just that by definition, these advances have made cars far more complex in addition to being safer and more efficient. That not only leads to more things that can break, but it also makes them harder for the backyard mechanic to trace and repair.


Brake testing has been a staple of *CR* testing since the 1950s. The hubcaps have been removed from this Oldsmobile to prevent losing them during testing maneuvers.


Consumer Reports


*Consumer Reports* stopped listing defects decades ago once it became apparent that some buyers were confusing delivery defects with long-term reliability, which are certainly two different things. It’s also fair to say that automaker quality control has improved to the point where *CR* hasn’t seen a loose steering box in years, even if some of their test cars still make multiple return trips to the dealer.


For most collectors, the decision to buy a vintage car is an emotional rather than a practical one. There’s nothing wrong with that, but it can make us look at our cars with rose-colored glasses and excuse some drawbacks. The reality is, an older vehicle is simply more likely to sputter to a stop at the side of the road than a new one. The difference is that an owner with basic mechanical knowledge may be able to make roadside repairs to an older car, when chances are a new one will have to wait for a tow truck.


The buttoned-up engineers of *CR* weren’t always focused on practical cars. Here, an MGA and an Alfa Romeo Giulietta slug it out in the dirt.


Consumer Reports


They may not make them like they used to, and that’s probably just as well. Older cars may not have been more reliable, but their relatively simple design and ease of repairability are part of the appeal, and why they’re still on the road. On the other hand, it remains to be seen how many of today’s vehicles will still be operational in another half century.
